title: Novel diagnostic pathways for prostate cancer risk assessment
official: Biomarker-enabled evaluation of novel diagnostic pathways for prostate cancer stratification and assessment
summary:
Background and study aims
Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men in the UK. Finding clinically significant prostate cancer at an early stage can improve treatment options and outcomes. However, current methods of assessing prostate cancer risk do not always identify the men most likely to have the disease.
This study aims to assess a new prostate cancer risk assessment pathway that combines a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test, a Stockholm3 blood test and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) when needed. Researchers want to find out how well this approach identifies clinically significant prostate cancer in routine UK clinical practice and whether it could help improve referral pathways and access to prostate cancer assessment services. 

Who can participate?
Men aged 45 to 74 years can take part if they:
• Have not previously been diagnosed with prostate cancer
• Are able to provide informed consent
• Are undergoing prostate cancer assessment through the study pathway
Men cannot take part if they have previously been diagnosed with prostate cancer, cannot provide informed consent, have a reason why they cannot have an MRI scan, or have had certain urological procedures within the previous 6 weeks. 

What does the study involve?
Participants will undergo a PSA blood test as part of a prostate cancer risk assessment pathway. If certain criteria are met, they will also have a Stockholm3 blood test. This test combines PSA levels with other biological markers, genetic information and clinical details to estimate the risk of clinically significant prostate cancer.
Participants whose test results indicate a higher level of risk may be offered an MRI scan. If the MRI findings suggest that further investigation is needed, a prostate biopsy may be carried out through routine NHS or private healthcare services.
Researchers will collect information about participants' test results, investigations and clinical outcomes. The study plans to follow around 10,000 participants. Participation in the research study is voluntary and is separate from access to the clinical testing pathway. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may benefit from receiving a detailed assessment of their prostate cancer risk, which could help identify clinically significant prostate cancer at an earlier stage.
The study itself does not involve treatments. The tests and investigations used in the pathway may have some risks or inconveniences. Blood tests can cause temporary discomfort or bruising. MRI scans may be uncomfortable for some people, particularly those who are uncomfortable in enclosed spaces. Men who require a biopsy may experience side effects associated with that procedure, which will be explained by their healthcare team.
The information collected may help improve future prostate cancer risk assessment and diagnosis for other men. 

Where is the study run from?
The study is being run in England and is recruiting through Nuffield Health Barbican Medical Centre in London. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to September 2029. 

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by Prostate Cancer Research, Nuffield Health and the Information Security Forum. 

Who is the main contact?
Dr Celine Kowalska, ckowalska@pcr.org.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Male participants aged 45–74 years
2. No previous diagnosis of prostate cancer
3. Ability to provide informed consent
4. Undergoing prostate cancer assessment through the study pathway
Exclusion criteria:
1. Previous diagnosis of prostate cancer
2. Inability to provide informed consent
3. Contraindication to prostate MRI
4. Previous urological procedure within 6 weeks of blood draw (e.g. cystoscopy, prostate biopsy or urethral catheterisation)
